comparable_sales.name: Comparable Sales Method (Market Approach)
comparable_sales.description: The Direct Comparison Method, also referred to as the Market Comparison Approach, is based on the principle of substitution, which holds that a prudent purchaser will not pay more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable alternative with similar utility. Under this method, the value of the subject property is derived by analysing recent sales and asking prices of comparable properties within the same or similar neighbourhoods. The comparables are selected based on similarity in location, use, tenure, size, physical characteristics, and market conditions. Adjustments are made to the sale prices of the comparable properties to reflect differences between the subject property and the comparables, including but not limited to location, plot size, building quality, condition, accessibility, services, and date of transaction.b After making appropriate adjustments, the analysed prices are reconciled to arrive at an indicative market value for the subject property. This method is consistent with the requirements of the RICS Valuation – Global Standards (Red Book) and is widely adopted by the Ghana Institution of Surveyors where sufficient and reliable market evidence exists.
comparable_sales.when_to_use: Most applicable when there are sufficient recent sales of similar properties in the area. Particularly suitable for residential properties and vacant land.
comparable_sales.template:
Comparable Sales Method (Market Approach)

Methodology Overview

The Comparable Sales Method, also known as the Market Approach or Sales Comparison Approach, estimates the value of the subject property by comparing it to similar properties that have recently sold in the same or similar localities.

This approach is based on the principle of substitution, which holds that a prudent purchaser would pay no more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equivalent substitute property with the same utility.

Selection of Comparables

In selecting comparable properties, the following criteria were considered:

  • Location and neighbourhood characteristics
  • Physical characteristics (size, age, condition, quality)
  • Legal characteristics (tenure, encumbrances)
  • Economic characteristics (income potential, occupancy)
  • Date of sale (currency of transaction)

income_approach.name: Income Approach (Investment Method)
income_approach.description: The Income Capitalisation Approach is premised on the principle that the value of an income-producing property is directly related to the income it is capable of generating over its useful life. This method is particularly applicable to investment and commercial properties such as offices, retail properties, hotels, and rental apartments. The valuation process involves estimating the Potential Gross Income (PGI) that the property can generate under normal market conditions. Allowances are then made for vacancy and collection losses to arrive at the Effective Gross Income (EGI). From the Effective Gross Income, all reasonable operating expenses necessary to maintain the property and generate the income are deducted to derive the Net Operating Income (NOI). Financing costs, income taxes, and capital expenditures are excluded in accordance with standard valuation practice. The Net Operating Income is then capitalised using an appropriate capitalisation rate or discounted using a discounted cash flow model, depending on the nature of the income stream and market evidence. This approach is in line with RICS and GhIS valuation standards and reflects market behaviour for income-producing real estate.
income_approach.when_to_use: Most suitable for properties that generate rental income or have income potential, such as commercial buildings, hotels, and investment properties.
income_approach.template:
Income Approach (Investment Method)

Methodology Overview

The Income Approach, also known as the Investment Method, estimates the value of a property based on the income it generates or is capable of generating. This approach is founded on the principle that the value of an income-producing property is directly related to the present value of its anticipated future benefits (income stream).

The method involves capitalizing the net income at an appropriate yield or capitalization rate derived from market evidence.

cost_approach.name: Cost Approach (Depreciated Replacement Cost)
cost_approach.description: The Cost Method estimates the value of a property by reference to the cost of constructing the improvements, assuming a modern equivalent, together with the value of the underlying land. The method involves estimating the current construction cost of the buildings using prevailing market rates and construction standards, including allowances for professional fees and contingencies where appropriate. Depreciation is then assessed to reflect the age, condition, design efficiency, and remaining economic life of the improvements. The depreciated cost of the buildings is added to the market value of the land to arrive at the overall capital value of the property. This approach is consistent with professional valuation practice and is commonly applied where income or direct market evidence is limited.
cost_approach.when_to_use: Most applicable for new or relatively new properties, special purpose properties, properties with limited market transactions, or where insurance value is required.
cost_approach.template:
Cost Approach (Depreciated Replacement Cost Method)

Methodology Overview

The Cost Approach, also known as the Contractor's Method or Depreciated Replacement Cost (DRC) Method, estimates the value of a property by calculating the cost of constructing a replacement building of equivalent utility, less accumulated depreciation, plus the value of the land.

This approach is based on the principle of substitution, which states that no rational buyer would pay more for an existing property than the cost of acquiring a similar site and constructing improvements of equivalent utility.

residual_method.name: Residual Method (Development Approach)
residual_method.description: The Residual Method is used primarily for development and redevelopment properties. It is based on the principle that the value of land or property is equal to the gross development value of the completed project less all costs associated with achieving that development. The process involves estimating the Gross Development Value (GDV) of the completed development based on prevailing market values or rental evidence. From this, deductions are made for construction costs, professional fees, statutory charges, finance costs, developer’s profit, and contingencies. The balance remaining after all deductions represents the residual value of the land or property in its current state. Due to its sensitivity to assumptions, the Residual Method is applied with caution and is supported by market evidence and professional judgement in line with RICS and GhIS standards.
residual_method.when_to_use: Most suitable for development sites, land with development potential, or properties requiring major refurbishment.
residual_method.template:
Residual Method (Development Approach)

Methodology Overview

The Residual Method, also known as the Development or Hypothetical Development Method, is used to assess the value of land or property with development potential. The method works backwards from the estimated value of the completed development, deducting all costs of development including developer's profit, to arrive at the residual land value.

profits_method.name: Profits Method
profits_method.description: The Profit Method is applied to properties where value is closely linked to the trading potential of the business conducted on the premises rather than to rental evidence. Examples include hotels, cinemas, leisure facilities, and certain hospitality properties. Under this method, the valuer assesses the maintainable gross income of the business based on historical accounts, industry benchmarks, and market expectations. From this, working expenses are deducted to arrive at a divisible balance. The divisible balance is then apportioned between the operator’s share (reward for entrepreneurship) and the landlord’s share, which is capitalised to determine the value of the property interest. The Profit Method requires careful judgement and is applied in accordance with RICS and GhIS guidance, ensuring that only property-related income is capitalised and that business risk is appropriately reflected.
profits_method.when_to_use: Applicable to specialized trading properties such as hotels, petrol stations, restaurants, cinemas, and other businesses where value is tied to trading potential.

Profits Method

Methodology Overview

The Profits Method is used to value properties where the value is primarily derived from the trading potential of the business carried on at the premises.
